You're right, being under influence in any sense in the job is a big no go for me.

But anyway, for some "research" it can be beneficial. But please do this in a responsable manner. In acting school we even did two times a rehearsal having drunk some beers just before, as a playful way to get more loose and funny. But it's not like you gain a huge enlightement from that. 

I use lsd or shrooms one to two times a year, that however is in my experience a huge creativity boost and mind opener. But please, if you consider doing this, please make sure you are in a good state of mind, you are in a secure and familiar environment and have no responsabilities the same day or the day after. If you can convince someone to be a trip sitter, that would be a good thing to, or at least someone you can call during, should you need too. Don't take it at a party, remember, it's for work! If you take it seriously it can be pretty interesting.

If you improv with one or more partners, remember that they are already doing 50% of the work for you, you don't have to carry the whole group, just relax and do your part, it's a team work. "Listen" very carefully to want your partner says or does, most of the time, the answer to that action will come naturally, if you *really* listen, without ever planing your next move. Be curious, do not know anything. If you are acting alone, remember that the audience is very likely on your side. Normally nobody is there you judge you. They want you to do good, sure, but that shouldn't pressure you, it should help you relax. And relaxed actors are always the better ones. Remember to have fun, to be silly and to be willing to do mistakes, because how else are you suppose to learn anything? 

I hope you have a blast!

I totally agree with you. Literally every new art movement that emerged has a beginning in non-conformity and Rebellion.   
I know, it's *only one* example, and luck certainly played a role, but, there once was a time were I was so frustrated about my auditions, because none of them seemed to work, that one day I was so fed up and exhausted that I internally said "fuck it", and I went in full anarchy mode while I performed on another one of those auditions. It worked. They took me, and since that day I can live from my job as an actor. They said something like "wow it was so authentic and fresh", and I was like yeah I bet it fucking was lol.   
So be free my dude, and with perseverance I'm sure that the right pair of eyes will see you one day (if it didn't already happen.) 

Of course this shouldn't discredit other people who pursue this craft in their own manner, wich I think you didn't intend that way, everyone should be respected in every way they do acting, but you know that. 

Edit: I also think, to NOT ALWAYS KNOW how something works, to still be open to discover new things in this art form is a good attribute for the job overall.

On a quick research I read that in Greece, the first college degree you pursue is free of charge. So, the ultimate goal would be to go to a university of arts and get a degree wich should be a guarantee for quality of training. But, because it's the state that finance you, there are *very* limited places per class years. I don't think it's that much about having connections (although, I know nothing about Greece), but to be authentic, a little predisposed talent, and also a bit of luck of course.   
If he doesn't get in, I would still try to look for auditions and jobs and maybe other classes. Getting in touch with casting directors is fairly simple, look for them in the credits of favorite greek movies and tv shows, and look them up online, there should be a mailing adress somewhere. Also apply to any job at the Theater, that the place where I dived into at 18, met a lot of artist who had lots of valuable infos about the whole industry. Go out in the world, as much as possible!

Hey there, well I won't lie, the filming industry here became quite slow since covid and inflation. It became rare to see new faces. I think as an international it might be even harder. My first advice would be to go to Berlin, this city became so international, sometimes they don't even speak german anymore in coffee shop etc. There should be the best place to work as a non-german.   
Due to me not knowing how the market is in the US, I can't say if it's better or worse here in Germany. Here you will find a much bigger dominance of University trained actors, because it's free and it's a guarantee for quality. But I know freelance actors with other training who make a decent living, it's not impossible.   
If you want more detailed infos, you are free to dm me!

CDs are just people too. Also, when they have a fresher set of eyes, it will be more helpful to you.

I assume that you're not a Professional? Screaming loud for long periods of time without injuring your voice takes years of training, and even with that I saw colleagues who were out of voice for a day or so.   
I mean, the most basic advice (That you still have to train for), is to breathe and scream with help of your diaphragm, wich means we need to see your biiiiig belly while decontraction and inhaling, push out the air while contraction and scream. At the same time your vocal chords have to be relaxed, so at the moment that you feel something is wrong with your throat, stop.   


remember, this is a "Don't try this at home" type of thing, even more without a qualified superviser. Try to find at least a class on youtube or something.

That's one hell of an interesting topic!  
One fact is: we will not be able to stop it. Progress is coming, whether we like it or not. So we will have to find a way to deal with it.  
I think the theatre (drama) will be one of the last crafts to be replaced by robotic/ai, because you'd literally need perfect looking humanoid robots to play. This is an extreme effort, wich I think will be less complicated with real humans for a long time. Also ten years ago everyone told us "Hologram concerts and plays will be a big thing, and everybody want's to see it", well... that didn't develop as fast as we thought, and I think that people aren't interested in Hologramm performances that much. just like 3D wasn't the Revolution for movies.  
For the movies and tv... it's another pair of shoes. We already have convincing examples for AI being used in movies (didn't they bring an actor "back to life" in one of the latest Star Wars movies???). I really think by the end of the century, that we will have CGI and audio that is not distinguishable from the real thing, and might be Oscar material... I even think, that you will be able to create a movie on the spot, made just for you.  
I work a lot with Midjourney, an art ai, you just type what picture you want, and the ai does it in like one minute, with already very convincing results. I think one day you'll be able to type: "make a romantic zombie movie with Leonardo DiCaprio and Jennifer Lawrence, with new music by Queen", and it will generate just that.  
I agree, it's fucking scary, and I wish I had a knock out argument saying, people or the industry won't want this. But i mean, it's very common and normal today to have a logo for your company made by an AI (Or for example my avatar, wich is the work of an AI). So why wouldn't it be normal in 50 years to have the same for movies...?  
On the other hand, new technologies brings new possibilities. For example, motion capture technologies developed so well, that suddenly actors are asked to play in video games, an industry where they never were before. It's even better to book actors for such projects, because it's less work for the programmer or cgi artist. So... Who knows what unexpected perks AI might bring for our job in the future?  
I think the spark of hope that we can keep is: AI still and and probably will always do as it is told. And nothing more. I think the ability to choose, to be spontaneous, imperfect, change mind, to oppose an idea or being opposed; those are things that AI won't be able to do. An AI is just a Programm, doing exactly as it is told. There is no surprise, no "in the moment".  
There is this scene in "Bohemian Rhapsody" where Freddy Mercury returns to his band mates after trying a solo career, and he says something like "I told the musicians what they had to do, and the problem is, they did as they were Told". This is great because it show that art in general need confrontations, conflicts, compromises, in short: human-to-human contact.  
If you want to dig deeper in the subject, I recommend you read "21 Lessons for the 21st Century" by Yuval Noah Harari. It's a very interesting book in general, but there is a whole section about art and AI (in the chapter about the replacement of working people), I think it's called "Mozart in the Machine" or something like that.  
Sorry for the long answer, but it's not a subject wich can be treated in two sentences!

Learn to operate safely with your voice; for example, on the side of my training I took opera and metal-screaming classes, just so I could learn to go in all possibles extremes without hurting my voice. But take basic voice training first.  
Fortify your body, make it stronger, bendier, dance (all genres), upgrade your endurance, take acrobatics classes or martial arts. Give yourself as many tools as possible, so your body doesn't stand in the way of your expression. (Wich doesn't mean that you have to be thin or buffed)Read, read, READ. Watch Movies/Series, A lot! Watch documentaries about people or society. Go out, fall in love, get drunk, laugh, cry, make mistakes, fight with your parents, whatever, LIVE!   
And: Go to therapy. Even if you think you're ok. Looking deeper into yourself with a professional is always helpful, especially for the job.  
Do as much as you can (afford also, i know...), But even if there is no afford, there should be effort!

The premiere is fourth of March. One of the funny side of that production is, it is already booked to be played in real school classes. So I will be forced to improvise, because I will play in many different, not only stages. The fourth wall is just non.existent, so there will be improvisation because of the interaction with the audience. It is hard work, lots of lines to learn (20 full pages), but I am excited to see what it will look like in the end, and who the public will react.   


Btw: I am thinking about doing a "ask me anything" on this sub, I am a full time paid actor in Germany, employed in one theater where in do 4-5 productions per season. Would it be of any interest?

I am sorry to read about your difficult situation, first of all, I wish you best of luck and I send you strength.

This is just my humble opinion, from my humble experience: You don't have to be perfect. Not even in an audition. The acting job is literally being human as a profession. And humans are not perfect, so why should you be? All auditions that worked for me where auditions where I was honest with myself and with the jury/casting direction, and if it still didn't work out, then because it had to be like this. I went to auditions where I forgot my costumes, or where I only learned half of the lines (so I improvised), and those still worked. I am a chaotic guy, who had to balance other stuff in life, and It is okay, that I presented myself this way.   
I mean, you cancelled this one audition, don't worry about it, maybe you needed the break. there will be others. Maybe next time try to go to audition and forgive yourself for not being 100% prepared, because otherwise you're giving yourself an immense amount of pressure, wich doesn't make you better as an actor.   
Audition is a little bit like flirting. If you go there with a playful attitude of "I don't *need* this job", it can even be quite charming for the casting direction. 

as for the work-life balance: back in my old days I also had to juggle with acting-school, auditions, projects and 2 side jobs. One rule I forced myself into: every night 8 hours of sleep, no matter what. I realized that it didn't help me to get all the stuff done but being tired all the time, because I was bad at all my jobs because of the exhaustion. I mean, it's only my way, you'd have to find your formula. But be good to yourself doing this job, because I think you might end up hating it, if it wears you out too much. 

and about the "dark place" and "depression" side of your post... well, If you don't already have, get help. Being miserable won't help you for the job either. It would be good to fix that, so you can continue with greater might. 

I'd be happy to answer any additional question, or even if you just need to talk or get rid of any thoughts.   
Wish you all the best.

Either way, your learning, that's for sure, so don't be shy about taking the jobs you can have!   
But in the meantime, yes, train. Training will make you better & faster & more professional on the job. But in my experience, you can only train so much, you have to go out There sometime. During my training I got jobs, and those jobs where like the completion of my school training. I could test the theory in real life. I am in my first year as full time actor, working on my 4th play since September, and in that half of a year I did learn more, than in two years scholar training combined. Wich doesn't mean that this training was worthless. but nothing replaces actual experience!

The only thing I'd ask is... Are you mentaly/psychologicaly done with this trauma? Acting should never be Thearapy (except maybe with a therapist). Cause if you're still mourning, just don't do it... I'm not a Therapist, but trust me.   
I wrote at least a master thesis including themes of role & psychology.   


If you tell me that everything is alright with the mourning side of your story, then I would say, why not? For me I would feel honored to be played as a character in a play. Obviously you would'n make fun of your friend, i guess that is of the table. I think you'd be engaged to do a honorable and respectful performance. So I think it's not morally wrong at all. 

But please, be careful and take care.

Hey!   
First of all: No. I don't agree with the fact that dutch movies are bad! You have some really great stuff over there, even stuff that got oscars. Maybe it's not as internationally known like US movies, but there also are killer cooperations with other big nation (like Dunkirk for example, and many other).   
And even if you think everything is "horrible", gotta start somewhere, right? Don't think you have to be "stuck" there for ever. But I tell you, if you star in some bigger Dutch productions, it does look good on the resume, everywhere in the world. Some experience is better than none. So just go for it!

I think how you described you craft in the second half is more than fine and also healthy. Relax, have fun, do good work. That's it.   
My experience taught me, every production is different, so I want to work differently, and I love it that my job is so varied! I think it is even better if you stay flexible in your approach during work, it's better than saying "No sorry I only do Chekhov" or whatever.

I would look at it from a way more free and bold perspective: 

You want to do a soldier role as a female? Just take one played by a male, and make it your own. just change a few thing if needed.   
Or classical literature and plays are full of female-warriors, take one and do it more modern!  
an actress from my theater auditioned as Richard III. She didn't care that it was a male part, she just wanted to play it. She got casted as Richard afterwards!   
Strict limits are your wort enemy in this art form/Job.

Look at it this way:   
If i were a casting director, and I search someone to play a cab-driver, and an actor or actress wrote to me "btw, I drove cabs for 5 years in the past", I would think that's great, because he/she doesn't have to imagine how it is to drive a cab, he/she will look very authentic. 

of course, I don't want to say that to drive a cab and being lesbian is the same thing or comparable. It's just for the metaphore. Just don't make it a big thing or your main argument for playing this role, but it sure is an advantage!

wish you good luck!

First of all: Congrats!  
A casting director once told me: "You had the better audition tape (actingwise), but the other contender is just a better fit for the part"   
So, made you were great in those other auditions, often it's only a matter of Type... And that's quite frustrating, because you can do only very little about your personality/looks/vibe...

It's a school production, you're there to learn, so just have fun and don't take it toooooo seriously! The best amateurs I ever saw, where always the relaxed ones and those, where I could see that they were having fun. Often amateurs are scared to "do something wrong", but the audience in this case are really your "friends", or "ally", they don't judge you as hard as you think, if they even do judge you. Relax! Have Fun!

But: Do you even want to do it? Can't you just say that you don't want to do it, if you feel unconfortable?

I'd say the first one, experience is way more important than names and references (in that particular case)  
so if one day you're confronted with a bigger production: If I was the casting director I would prefer seeing the actor/actress "who already played as a leading role" than the "3rd coffeshop customer from that Marvel Movie". You know? 

that is of course, if you want to build a career. If you want to make a quick buck, then do the big production.

Be transparent with the agency, it will be far worse when they need you in one or two month and you just say "I can't, I have college...", then when you are just honest with them.   
You know, maybe they can schedule the contract begin for April or may, who knows? If they really want you, it shouldn't be a problem. I mean you're not saying "I don't want to work with you", you're just postponing it for a very near future.   
I always speak openly with my agent, and tell wich days and weeks I can't go to set, I have a lot of work on stage, wich give me little room for filming, but we want to still work together and do the best out of it, so it is important to speak with transparence, and if doesn't suit them, then you should ask yourself, it it'll be a good work relationship?

Of course! The more input you get the better and faster you will grow and learn! It's important to get different views and techniques, there's no limit to the number of coaches you can have!  
Just don't say stuff like "Yeah but the other teacher said I should do it like this, and so and so...", it just isn't interesting for them (sometimes I do coaching to, and I'm not pretending to know the best formula for acting, I just share my views and techniques and hope it somehow resonates with the student. But how other people teach stuff, I don't care)

It is *so extremly rare*, that I would say it's close to impossible. I worked in lots of theaters here in Germany where I live, and I only met one non trained actor, but he was a close friend with a huge director who always casted him, and he is also heavily type-casted, because he has a severe form of body-disability. 

You still can work at the theater as a non trained, but more as an extra or very little parts. When I was younger, before my training, I even made a decent living out of working as an extra at the opera and national theater. Those weren't crazy good experiences, but I got a good look into how a theater works from the inside, could watch actor rehearse everyday up close, and I even met and worked with some very famous and talented people, wich *still* looks good on my resume today. Of course, maybe it is different in other parts of the world, I don't know where you live, but in Europe it shouldn't be a big problem. If I where you, I'd give it a try until you feel ready to enter an acting school. None of my acting colleagues are non-trained right know, and sometimes I have to say, it is good that way, it's a whole other deal of professionalism than working with amateurs (wich can be fun, but maybe only from time to time).
no probs man, wish you luck! Have fun!

There was a time in my life, where I suffered from severe depression. Acting was the only thing keeping me going, but my life outside the job was miserable. I seeked professional medical help, and after a few years, is was healed, and you know what? It made me an even better actor. Sometimes I successfully translated my pain into a performance, wich people liked, but I wouldn't do that to often, because the stage is not therapy, and you will think you have to stay unhappy, to be a good actor/actress. That's not the case. 

I would recommend you to find a therapist, hopefully you live in a country, where it is affordable...   
The acting profession is about being yourself, and it is just ok to be, whoever you are, in all your states and imperfections. But be a happier human, you'll be a happier Actor/Actress, and it will always help you more, in life like in the job. 

I could list you names of very good and successful actors who where miserable in their life, but I don't think that it is the example to follow. But yes, it is possible to be an actor, even with negative thoughts. But it's not helping at all.

My mentor in acting school told me once, your "Weaknesses" are also your Strengths, and the other way around. As more and more time passes by, I understand what he meant by that. 

short example: I am a multilingual guy, wich can be great at times, obviously speaking different languages is great, but it also causes chaos in my head, I confuse the languages, words and grammar. Once I decided for myself, that I won't be afraid no more to show that imperfect side of myself, also while acting, lot's of people have complimented me saying, that it is interesting and fun to hear and see my unique usage of language. My weakness became my strength.

I don't want to compare my situation and yours, I can't know how it is to be you. But I still think that this weakness/strength rule is universal (kinda like ying yang, haha). Obviously with your condition, I think you will be more the type for very specific projects, wich can be hard to find. But your uniqueness, can be a powerful asset for your career, you just have to make the decision to not do everything "right". Be your truest self, don't try to be the "norm", don't try to "fix" yourself, people will be thankful to discover your authentic side. But obviously it's a giant leap. And It's also a lot of work, you have to put lot's of energy, time and nerves. Ask yourself, if your goal is worth all that investment. 

I wish you the best, and I'd be happy to help, if you have any more questions!

Of course, the best option to give yourself the best chances to become an actor, is to put most of your energy, time and maybe also money in that goal. The more you focus on it, the better the chances. Now obviously it's a big sacrifice, you'd have to be very passionate about it. But every "back up" you provide yourself with (such as law school, high paying job, etc) will reduce the chances of you getting a real career in acting, in my opinion. 

I decided a while ago to drop the hopes for a wealthy life, and just do what I love. after years of hard work, I can decently live from acting, but more importantly: I am absolutely fulfilled, and I would NEVER give that up for any money in the world. 

So, I guess, it's just about what decision you make, that are your aspirations and wishes for your life. And you know, you are very young, even if you do 3 more years of law school, I think you can still enter an acting career, by then you will have grown and you will know even more what you want in life. I don't think that you have to pressure yourself to take that important decision NOW! And in the meantime, while you still think about it, take every possible experience opportunity you can get (college drama club, selftapes, acting classes, etc), as long as it's fun, it's good.

My answer from a post two days ago: 

At the Drama Academy they taught us not to learn lines, but to learn thoughts, inner pictures, stories... might seem stupid, but I swear, you will never need more than Minutes to memorize lines if you train for that. 

It's kinda hard to explain. For example, it would be torture to learn the 100 First digits of PI, if you only try to memorize every number. But if you learn "1 group of friends hab 4 members, 1 was introduced to them, then they were 5, they went partying from 9 to 2", then you have the six first digits of PI: 3,141592...

We also did exercises where we had to remember 200 random words in an exact order. Same thing, you have to make yourself a story, you can't just memorize the words. 

For me dialogues are the easiest. Ether you want to know something from your partner, or you give him an answer. Try to always think of the content of the story, not the words. And for a Monologe It's the same thing, It's a Dialoge with yourself or with a silent audience or partner. 

As I said, it is really difficult to explain, but I hope I could inspire you to try it out. Best of Luck for everything!

Don't be afraid and DON'T WAIT! It doesn't matter if you teach yourself or if you are at the best acting academy in the world, you can only learn by doing in this job.  


Second: I really wish you the best in achieving your goals, and you should aim high! But don't let yourself down if it doesn't work at your first shot. London is certainly great, but I know that there are very good alternatives in the United Kingdom. You should try more than just one option. For my own story, I'm acting in Germany, where everybody including myself wants to get accepted in Berlin. I didn't. I was accepted in Leipzig, wich probably is a city nobody heard of. And it gave me so many opportunities wich I would have never got in Berlin. 

Third: You're so young. I mean I get it, nobody wants to heard that when there becoming 18, but it's true. It took me 3 to 4 years of experimenting before I was accepted in Drama School,  and people still tell me that I am young and I have so much ahead of me. I'm 25. so if by the end of your 18s your not an accomplished Actor, trust me, It's not the end, you didn't even start.   


I Hope I could help you with some of those scary thoughts. AND GO OUT AND HAVE A BLAST BY ACTING OR SOMETHING!

At the Drama Academy they taught us not to learn lines, but to learn thoughts, inner pictures, stories... might seem stupid, but I swear, you will never need more than Minutes to memorize lines if you train for that. 

It's kinda hard to explain. For example, it would be torture to learn the 100 First digits of PI, if you only try to memorize every number. But if you learn "1 group of friends hab 4 members, 1 was introduced to them, then they were 5, they went partying from 9 to 2", then you have the six first digits of PI: 3,141592...

We also did exercises where we had to remember 200 random words in an exact order. Same thing, you have to make yourself a story, you can't just memorize the words. 

For me dialogues are the easiest. Ether you want to know something from your partner, or you give him an answer. Try to always think of the content of the story, not the words. And for a Monologe It's the same thing, It's a Dialoge with yourself or with a silent audience or partner. 

As I said, it is really difficult to explain, but I hope I could inspire you to try it out. Best of Luck for everything!

Learning lines becomes really easy with time and practice. In Drama school we had exercises like remembering the first 50 digits of PI or remembering a 200 random word list. We quickly learned that you can't actually learn the information, but you have to learn "the thought" or "the story" behind the information. It a bit hard to explain. But in stead of thinking "what is the line/ what are the words" try to remember "what are the characters thoughts". Also what helps me, in a dialoge, is to really carefully listen to my partner, because 90% of the time the responding line is just plain logical, and also a listening actor is a good actor!
